caption:
Google opened preorders for its Gemini glasses, made with Warby Parker and Gentle Monster and built by Samsung.
They start at $395, have a camera, speakers and "Hey Gemini" built in, and ship December 10.
There is no screen, and a light shows when the camera records.

Would you wear glasses with an AI and a camera in them?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

Source: 9to5Google, Unite.AI · Photo: Google
threads_text: Google's Gemini glasses are up for preorder: $395 with Warby Parker, $449 with Gentle Monster, in stores December 10. Camera, open-ear speakers, "Hey Gemini", no screen, and they work with iPhone too. Would you actually wear these?

slides.headline: Google just opened preorders for its Gemini glasses. They start at *$395* and ship December 10

slides.heading: Two brands, *30 designs*
paras: Warby Parker's three frames start at $395. Gentle Monster's six frames start at $449. Samsung builds the hardware.
Preorders opened on November 12. Stores and shipping start December 10, in the US and South Korea.

slides.heading: Just say *Hey Gemini*
paras: Ask Gemini about what you are looking at, get Google Maps directions or live translation in over 70 languages.
There is no screen. A 12MP camera and open-ear speakers do the work.

slides.heading: A light you *can't hide*
paras: A light shows when the camera records. If it is covered, recording stops.
Google says faces of people nearby are blurred before Gemini sees them, and camera images are not used for AI training or ads.

slides.heading: Works with *iPhone too*
paras: They pair with Pixel 7 and newer, recent Galaxy phones and iPhone 13 Pro and newer.
Up to 9 hours of battery, and the case recharges them 7 times.

slides.hook: Follow to see how Google's glasses stack up against Meta's when they ship on December 10.

paragraphs.text: Google opened preorders on November 12, 2026 for its Gemini-powered Intelligent Eyewear, a line of smart glasses designed with the eyewear brands Warby Parker and Gentle Monster and engineered by Samsung, according to 9to5Google and Unite.AI. Shipping and in-store availability begin on December 10.

Warby Parker's frames start at $395 and Gentle Monster's at $449, with Android Headlines putting the top Gentle Monster models at $489. Android Headlines counted 30 designs in total: 14 Warby Parker variations across three frames and 16 Gentle Monster variations across six frames.

Warby Parker's three styles are called Alden, Reid and Wren, offered in optical and sun versions in Pine, Saddle and Jet Black, 9to5Google reported. Gentle Monster's six frames come in colors that include dark red, pink, gray and yellow, with clear, tinted, blue or brown lenses, and prescriptions are available for most designs. Unite.AI reported that more than 360 Warby Parker stores will offer guided demos, along with selected partner and Google Store locations.

The glasses have no display. They rely on a 12 megapixel ultra-wide camera that records video at up to 3K, four microphones and two open-ear speakers, running on a Qualcomm Snapdragon AR1 Gen 1 chip, according to 9to5Google. The frames weigh 40 to 44 grams, the battery is rated at nine hours, and the charging case holds seven full charges.
What Gemini does on the glasses

Wearers can wake the assistant with a new Hey Gemini phrase, a tap on the frame or, with a Pixel Watch, a hand gesture. Google lists questions about objects in view, turn-by-turn directions from Google Maps and real-time speech translation through Google Translate in more than 70 languages. The speakers also work as headphones for music, calls and spoken message summaries.

Unite.AI reported that Google's accessibility feature Guided Vision, which gives spoken descriptions of surroundings to blind and low-vision users, will also run on the glasses with a compatible Android phone. Google says the feature can make mistakes and is not a mobility aid.

An outward-facing light turns on when the camera captures a photo or video, and recording stops if the light is covered or disabled, 9to5Google reported. Google says faces of bystanders are automatically redacted before Gemini processes what the camera sees, and that those camera visuals are not saved to Gemini History or used for AI training or ad targeting. A physical switch turns off the camera, microphones and Gemini.

Google Play rules bar apps on the glasses from using the camera for real-time facial identification, according to Unite.AI. Android Headlines reported that buyers must be 18 or older and pass age verification to activate the glasses.
The glasses work with Pixel 7 phones and newer, Galaxy S, Z Fold and Z Flip models on One UI 9.0 or later, and iPhone 13 Pro and newer, according to 9to5Google and Android Headlines.

The launch puts Google in direct competition with Meta's Ray-Ban glasses in the same form: a camera, speakers and an assistant inside frames that look like ordinary eyewear. Supporting iPhones from day one and leading with privacy controls suggests Google wants to reach buyers beyond its own phone users and answer the camera concerns that followed earlier smart glasses.
The first reviews after the December 10 release should show whether the nine hour battery claim and the bystander face redaction hold up in daily use.
